kaigo-foundation-01-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Introduce your name, profession and assignment, and check how the person would like to be addressed.
Check whether it is a convenient time to talk, and distinguish matters that need to be referred to another professional.

kaigo-foundation-01-knowledge-0.heading: The roles of care workers and other professionals
paragraphs: Care workers support daily life, notice changes from a person’s usual condition and share their observations with the team. Doctors diagnose and treat illness; nurses provide nursing care and assist with medical care. Care workers cannot independently take over diagnosis or treatment.

Physical therapists (PTs) support basic movements such as standing and walking. Occupational therapists (OTs) support activities needed in daily life. Speech-language therapists (STs) support functions such as speaking and swallowing. Each profession contributes its expertise toward the same person’s goals.

kaigo-foundation-01-knowledge-1.heading: Who to consult about food, daily life and services
paragraphs: Dietitians and nutritionists specialize in nutrition and meals. Care managers help plan and coordinate services based on the person’s wishes and living situation. Professionals who provide advice and support, such as social workers, help with everyday difficulties and available systems and resources.

For example, eating less and finding a spoon difficult to use may occur together, but the cause is not yet known. Share the observed facts and consult the relevant professionals about both food and nutrition and daily activities. If swallowing difficulty is suspected, refer the concern to a nurse or speech-language therapist rather than choosing exercises yourself.

kaigo-foundation-01-knowledge-2.heading: What to say when introducing yourself
paragraphs: Begin with your name, profession and assignment for the day. Then ask how the person would like to be addressed and whether now is a good time to talk. Even when trying to be friendly, do not drop respectful forms of address or choose childish names without checking the person’s preference.
Explain which support you can provide and which matters require another professional. Knowing the names of professions does not authorize you to promise treatment or decide on an exercise method.

kaigo-foundation-01-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Tanaka, a newly assigned care worker, visits Morikawa’s room. Explain your role so you are not mistaken for a nurse, then check the preferred form of address and whether there is time to talk.

kaigo-foundation-01-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Tanaka, a newly assigned care worker, visits Morikawa’s room. Explain your role so you are not mistaken for a nurse, then check the preferred form of address and whether there is time to talk.
Haruko Morikawa: Are you starting here today?
Care worker: Yes, I’m Tanaka, a care worker. I’m assigned to your room today. It’s nice to meet you.
Haruko Morikawa: So you’re not a nurse?
Care worker: That’s right, I’m a care worker. If you’d like to speak to a nurse, I can put you in touch with the nurse responsible.
Haruko Morikawa: I see. I’m Morikawa. Please call me Haruko-san.
Care worker: Haruko-san—of course, I’ll call you that. Would now be a good time for a short chat?
Haruko Morikawa: Yes, but please leave a longer conversation for later.
Care worker: Of course. I’ll just introduce myself today. We can talk another time when it suits you.

kaigo-foundation-01-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] You are greeting someone who wishes to be addressed by their surname. They have two minutes before a phone call.
Approach: Introduce your profession and assignment, and confirm the preferred surname and that you will keep the greeting brief. No specialist advice has been requested.
Example response: I’m Tanaka, a care worker. I’ll use your surname as you prefer. Could I take about two minutes just to say hello before your call?
Limits of support: The goal is to check preferences about the form of address and available time. Do not add medical advice.

kaigo-foundation-01-reading.heading: Read records and messages
paragraphs: Today’s assigned care worker is Tanaka. Morikawa wishes to be addressed as “Haruko-san” and requested only a brief greeting today.

kaigo-language-transfer-240.heading: What to do together and what to leave to staff
paragraphs: [Text created for learning] Person receiving care: “I’d like us to choose the vegetables together. I’d like the staff to do the cooking.” Care worker: “Let’s confirm that division of tasks.”

kaigo-foundation-02-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Ask about the person’s wishes, and check consent for the task and for moving personal belongings separately.
Explain dignity, quality of life and the right to participate through everyday situations.

kaigo-foundation-02-knowledge-0.heading: Dignity and quality of life
paragraphs: A person’s worth does not change with the amount of assistance they need. Respect each person as an individual, understand their habits, relationships, culture and wishes, and avoid imposing staff preferences.

Quality of life (QOL) is not simply the number of tasks someone can complete. Consider satisfaction, enjoyment, purpose and how the person feels about life. Even someone who manages personal care independently may feel lonely or dissatisfied; those feelings still need to be heard.

kaigo-foundation-02-knowledge-1.heading: The right to participate and individual support
paragraphs: Normalization is the idea that people should have their rights protected and be able to live in their own way in the community, whether or not they have a disability. It does not mean making everyone follow the same lifestyle.

People joining the same activity may need different ways of getting there, different explanations or different levels of help. Check their wishes and adjust conditions that prevent participation. A different method of participating does not mean a different right to participate.

kaigo-foundation-02-knowledge-2.heading: Choices that matter to the individual
paragraphs: Some people would rather listen quietly to familiar music than join a large group game. Ask what they look forward to and what conditions would make participation appealing. The facility’s schedule supports everyday life; making people follow it is not itself the goal of care.

kaigo-foundation-02-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] There is a newspaper and a pair of glasses on Hasebe’s table. Before wiping the table, check whether to do it now, where to put the belongings and what to do afterward. Consent to cleaning does not mean permission to move personal belongings however you choose.

kaigo-foundation-02-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] There is a newspaper and a pair of glasses on Hasebe’s table. Before wiping the table, check whether to do it now, where to put the belongings and what to do afterward. Consent to cleaning does not mean permission to move personal belongings however you choose.
Kenichi Hasebe: The table is a little dirty.
Care worker: Would you like me to wipe the table now, or leave it until later?
Kenichi Hasebe: Now, please. But I’m still reading the newspaper.
Care worker: You’re still reading it, then. Where would you like me to put it while I wipe the table?
Kenichi Hasebe: Please don’t put it under the shelf. Put it on the chair next to me, with the glasses beside it.
Care worker: The newspaper and glasses on the chair next to you, is that right? May I move them there and then wipe the table?
Kenichi Hasebe: Yes. Please put the newspaper back afterward.
Care worker: Of course. I’ll put the newspaper back once I’ve finished wiping. Would you like the glasses back in their original place too?
Kenichi Hasebe: Yes, both, please.
Care worker: Certainly. I’ll start now.

kaigo-foundation-02-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] The person has agreed to having the table wiped but wants the glasses left where they are.
Approach: Confirm that the glasses should stay in place and ask which area you may clean first.
Example response: You’d like the glasses to stay here, is that right? May I start with the part of the table where there are no glasses?
Limits of support: Consent to cleaning does not imply consent to moving every belonging.

kaigo-foundation-02-reading.heading: Read records and messages
paragraphs: Hasebe requested that the table be cleaned. During cleaning, the newspaper and glasses will be placed on the adjacent chair. It was confirmed with Hasebe that both will be returned to their original positions afterward.

kaigo-language-transfer-252.heading: The order of explanation and consent
paragraphs: [Text created for learning] In this card, explain the purpose and what you will do, and check the person’s consent before changing the position.

kaigo-foundation-03-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Distinguish what the person wants to do, what they can do and what help they need.
Respect the person’s right to make decisions even when physical assistance is needed.

kaigo-foundation-03-knowledge-0.heading: Independence includes making decisions
paragraphs: Independence includes choosing how to live and making decisions, not just carrying out physical actions unaided. For example, someone who needs help fastening buttons can still choose what to wear and when to change.

To support independence, build on what the person can do, make the task easier to carry out and help with the parts that need support. Doing everything for them simply to save time may take away opportunities to use their abilities and feel in control.

kaigo-foundation-03-knowledge-1.heading: Connect an action with its purpose in daily life
paragraphs: Everyday life involves getting up, eating, toileting, bathing and resting, as well as health, housework, housing and relationships with family and the community. Daily rhythms and priorities differ from person to person.

Fastening a button to get ready to see a friend has a different meaning from changing clothes when there is no hurry. Instead of judging only the speed of the action, find out what the person hopes to achieve through it.

kaigo-foundation-03-knowledge-2.heading: Agree on the help that is needed
paragraphs: Ask what the person wants to do independently, which parts they want help with and how they would like to proceed. Afterward, check whether anything was difficult or whether they would like something done differently.
Do not conclude that a person can do nothing simply because they decline one action. When support needs to be reviewed, share both the person’s wishes and the observed situation with the team.

kaigo-foundation-03-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Onodera wants to write a postcard to a friend. There is no information about illness or movement abilities. Do not make assumptions based on age; ask which parts the person wants to write and which parts they want help with.

kaigo-foundation-03-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Onodera wants to write a postcard to a friend. There is no information about illness or movement abilities. Do not make assumptions based on age; ask which parts the person wants to write and which parts they want help with.
Fumi Onodera: I’d like to write a postcard to a friend.
Care worker: That sounds nice. Could you tell me which parts you’d like to write yourself and which parts you’d like help with?
Fumi Onodera: I’ll write the message myself. I’d just like you to read the address because the writing is small.
Care worker: You’ll write the message yourself, then. Is reading the address the only help you’d like?
Fumi Onodera: Yes, the address on this paper. Please read it slowly.
Care worker: Of course. I’ll read it in parts rather than all at once. Please let me know if you’d like me to repeat anything.
Fumi Onodera: Thank you. Once I’ve finished writing, I’ll check it myself.
Care worker: Of course, you’ll check it yourself too. Please let me know if you need anything else.

kaigo-foundation-03-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] The person wants to write their own schedule but asks you to read out the dates because the print is small.
Approach: Leave the writing to the person and check the reading speed and how to divide the information. Give them time to ask you to repeat anything.
Example response: You’ll write the schedule yourself, is that right? I’ll read the dates one at a time. Please let me know if you’d like me to repeat anything.
Limits of support: Do not change the schedule’s contents or write the whole thing for the person.

kaigo-foundation-03-reading.heading: Read records and messages
paragraphs: Onodera wishes to write the postcard message independently and check it personally afterward. The only help requested from staff is to read out the address on the paper slowly.

kaigo-language-transfer-242.heading: Use experience to take an active role
paragraphs: [Text created for learning] Person receiving care: “I can show you how to fold this bag.” Care worker: “Could you show me?” Person receiving care: “Yes, let’s sit down and do it.”

kaigo-foundation-04-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Choose a place where others will not overhear, and check which information may be shared and with whom.
Recognize physical restraint and abuse, and report facts to the appropriate contact.

kaigo-foundation-04-knowledge-0.heading: Protect privacy and confidential information
paragraphs: Respecting privacy includes avoiding unnecessary exposure of the body, choosing where to talk and considering who might overhear. Confidentiality means keeping within the permitted limits when collecting, using, storing and sharing personal information.

Consent to a conversation is not consent to taking a photograph or posting it on social media. Do not send records to staff members’ personal accounts; use approved work methods. This exercise concerns an ordinary consultation, not decisions about emergencies or legal exceptions.

kaigo-foundation-04-knowledge-1.heading: Consider what a restraint actually does
paragraphs: Physical restraint limits a person’s freedom to move or act. Examples of concern include tying limbs, using a belt to prevent standing, surrounding a bed with rails so the person cannot get out, locking someone in a room or using excessive medication to suppress activity.

Calling something a safety measure does not establish that it is appropriate. Restraint may harm physical function and mental or physical well-being. First review the environment and support methods, consult the team through established procedures and do not decide alone whether to use restraint.

kaigo-foundation-04-knowledge-2.heading: Recognize abuse and report facts
paragraphs: Abuse includes physical abuse, psychological abuse, neglect or abandonment of necessary care, financial abuse and sexual abuse. Look beyond physical violence: frightening words or actions, failure to provide necessary care and improper financial gain are also concerns.

If abuse is suspected, protect the person’s safety and report the facts to the designated reporting or advice contact. Do not conceal concerns because a colleague is involved. Separate what you saw or heard from assumptions, and do not conduct an investigation or reach conclusions on your own.

kaigo-foundation-04-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Morikawa wants to discuss a family matter. Do not ask for details in the hallway. Agree on a quiet place to talk and establish which information may be shared and with whom. There is no need to invent private family circumstances for this exercise.

kaigo-foundation-04-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Morikawa wants to discuss a family matter. Do not ask for details in the hallway. Agree on a quiet place to talk and establish which information may be shared and with whom. There is no need to invent private family circumstances for this exercise.
Haruko Morikawa: I’d like to talk about something to do with my family, but not in the hallway.
Care worker: I won’t ask about the details here. Would you like to talk in your room?
Haruko Morikawa: Yes. Please don’t tell my daughter about it yet.
Care worker: You don’t want your daughter told at this point, is that right? Let me first hear what you would like.
Haruko Morikawa: You may tell the assigned care worker if it’s necessary for the discussion.
Care worker: If we need to tell the assigned care worker, let’s first agree together on what to share.
Haruko Morikawa: That puts my mind at ease. I’ll talk in my room.
Care worker: Then I’ll listen there. Let’s make sure the conversation can’t be heard from the hallway.

kaigo-foundation-04-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] The person has agreed only to telling their daughter about a change in visiting time. They have not agreed to sharing the private discussion.
Approach: Confirm the recipient and message, and choose a place or method where others are unlikely to overhear.
Example response: I’ll tell your daughter only that the visiting time has changed, without including our other conversation. Is that all right?
Limits of support: Being a family member does not automatically entitle someone to the whole conversation. This is an ordinary communication situation.

kaigo-foundation-04-reading.heading: Read records and messages
paragraphs: Morikawa wishes to discuss a family matter. Details were not requested in the hallway, and it was agreed to talk in the room. Morikawa does not currently want the daughter contacted. If information needs to be shared with the assigned care worker, first agree with Morikawa on what may be shared.

kaigo-language-transfer-256.heading: A wish and the stages of safety checks
paragraphs: [Text created for learning] The person would like a bath. Checks of their condition and the equipment have not yet been carried out. After the person in charge checks them, the method will be discussed.

kaigo-foundation-05-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Separate the wish to participate from consent to being photographed, and do not promise unconfirmed arrangements.
Explain the differences between services and why outcomes must be reviewed in the care process.

kaigo-foundation-05-knowledge-0.heading: Where someone lives and how services are used
paragraphs: With visiting services, staff go to the place where the person lives. With day services, the person attends a service center during the day. With residential services, the person lives at the facility and receives support there. Look at where someone lives and how the service is used, rather than relying only on the building’s name.
Short stays are another possibility. Check the period of use and the individual plan; arriving at a service center does not by itself mean that the person has moved there.

kaigo-foundation-05-knowledge-1.heading: Review support through the care process
paragraphs: The care process involves gathering and considering information, making a plan, providing support and reviewing the outcome to help the person live as they wish. Assessment brings together wishes, abilities and the living environment to identify difficulties in daily life.

The plan sets goals and specifies support, which is then carried out. Afterward, evaluate progress toward the goals and whether the method still fits the person. If the situation changes, review the plan as a team. Marking a task as done is not the same as evaluating its outcome.

kaigo-foundation-05-knowledge-2.heading: Check the outcome of participation
paragraphs: For example, if the goal is to join a reading group, simply taking someone to the room does not establish success. Check whether they participated as they wished and whether they became tired or experienced difficulties.
Record what you observed and what the person said so the team can consider adjustments. A staff member should not change goals or the support plan alone.

kaigo-foundation-05-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Photographs are planned during an optional flower-planting activity. Onodera would like to join but does not want to be photographed. Treat these as two separate wishes and check whether participation without appearing in photographs is possible. Do not promise an unconfirmed seat or arrangement.

kaigo-foundation-05-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Photographs are planned during an optional flower-planting activity. Onodera would like to join but does not want to be photographed. Treat these as two separate wishes and check whether participation without appearing in photographs is possible. Do not promise an unconfirmed seat or arrangement.
Fumi Onodera: I’d like to join the flower planting, but I don’t want to be in any photos.
Care worker: You’d like to join, but you don’t want to be photographed, is that right?
Fumi Onodera: Yes. Is there somewhere I won’t be photographed?
Care worker: I don’t know yet. May I check with the activity coordinator?
Fumi Onodera: Please do. Just tell them what I’d like.
Care worker: I’ll tell them you don’t want to be photographed and ask what arrangements are possible for joining. The arrangements haven’t been decided yet.
Fumi Onodera: Then I’ll decide after I hear the answer.
Care worker: I’ll tell you what I find out and then ask again what you would like to do.

kaigo-foundation-05-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] The person wants to join a craft activity, but it is not yet known whether photography can be avoided.
Approach: Acknowledge both wishes and ask permission to check the participation arrangements with the person in charge.
Example response: You’d like to join but don’t want to be photographed, is that right? May I ask the person in charge what arrangements are possible?
Limits of support: Before receiving an answer, do not promise a place free from photography or guarantee participation.

kaigo-foundation-05-reading.heading: Read records and messages
paragraphs: Onodera would like to join flower planting but does not want to be photographed. Permission was obtained to ask the activity coordinator about participation arrangements. The arrangements remain unconfirmed, and the final decision about joining will be made after the answer is received.

kaigo-language-transfer-259.heading: Application deadlines and participation conditions
paragraphs: [Text created for learning] Applications for exhibition materials close on Thursday. You can still visit Saturday’s exhibition without applying for the materials.

kaigo-foundation-06-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Check each message separately, distinguishing confirmed information from information not yet checked.
Explain the reasons for standard precautions, changing gloves and hand hygiene.

kaigo-foundation-06-knowledge-0.heading: How infection can spread
paragraphs: In infection prevention, consider the source of infection, the route of transmission and the condition of the person who might become infected. Contact through hands or objects, droplets and airborne transmission require different precautions. Do not assume one method covers every situation.

If you notice fever, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, a rash or a change in complexion, observe what differs from the person’s usual condition and report it to a healthcare professional. Do not identify a pathogen from symptoms alone; follow the facility’s procedures.

kaigo-foundation-06-knowledge-1.heading: Standard precautions and protective equipment
paragraphs: Use standard precautions for everyone receiving care, not only people known to have an infection. Consider what you may contact and the risks of the task. Choose gloves, an apron or gown, a mask and eye protection according to the possibility of contact or splashes involving blood, body fluids, secretions or excretions.
Do not handle clean items or help another person while wearing gloves used for a dirty task. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, which is also needed after removing them.

kaigo-foundation-06-knowledge-2.heading: Choose between handwashing and hand rubbing
paragraphs: When hands are visibly dirty, wash with running water and soap, rinse thoroughly and dry them. When using an alcohol-based product, follow its instructions and the facility’s procedure, cover all areas of the hands and rub until dry. The same method is not suitable for every pathogen.

Check not only the palms but also the backs of the hands, between the fingers, the fingertips and around the nails, thumbs and wrists. Do not mix products yourself or wipe them off while rubbing them in.

kaigo-foundation-06-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] A colleague asks you to pass on information about library hours and returning a book. Separate the two matters and ask again about anything you did not hear clearly. Practice keeping confirmed information distinct from information that has not yet been checked.

kaigo-foundation-06-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] A colleague asks you to pass on information about library hours and returning a book. Separate the two matters and ask again about anything you did not hear clearly. Practice keeping confirmed information distinct from information that has not yet been checked.
Misaki Kishimoto: Could you pass on a message to Hasebe? It’s about the library hours and returning a book.
Care worker: Sorry, could you tell me those two things one at a time?
Misaki Kishimoto: The library is open until three today. The book doesn’t have to be returned today.
Care worker: So the library is open until three, and the book doesn’t have to be returned today, is that right?
Misaki Kishimoto: Yes. But I haven’t checked the return deadline yet.
Care worker: The deadline hasn’t been confirmed, then. I’ll make clear that the book doesn’t need to be returned today and that the deadline is still unconfirmed.
Misaki Kishimoto: Thank you. I’ll check the deadline and let you know later.
Care worker: You’ll be responsible for checking the deadline, then, Kishimoto. I’ll wait to hear from you once you’ve checked.

kaigo-foundation-06-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] The activity room can be used until 4 p.m. The program’s finishing time is still being checked.
Approach: Keep the confirmation status of the two times separate. Ask who will check the finishing time and when the result will be shared.
Example response: The room is available until 4 p.m., but the activity’s finishing time is still being checked, is that right? Who will check it, and when will you let us know?
Limits of support: Do not report the room’s usage limit as if it were the confirmed finishing time of the activity.

kaigo-foundation-06-reading.heading: Read records and messages
paragraphs: The library is open until 3 p.m. today. The book does not have to be returned today, but the return deadline has not been confirmed. Care worker Kishimoto will check the deadline and then pass on the information.

kaigo-language-transfer-234.heading: Task order in a practice situation
paragraphs: [Text created for learning] Senior colleague: “In this exercise, close the box before writing the name.” Care worker: “So I write the name and then close the box?” Senior colleague: “That’s the other way around.”

kaigo-foundation-07-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Respect the person’s choices, provide the help requested and pass on necessary information.
Explain conditions that reduce strain on the back, the need for assistive equipment, staff health and disaster preparedness.

kaigo-foundation-07-knowledge-0.heading: Body movement and strain on the lower back
paragraphs: The base of support is the area enclosed by the points supporting the body. Positioning the feet appropriately and considering the center of gravity can help stabilize posture. Working far from the body can increase strain on the lower back, so adjust the working position and height.

Rather than relying on arm strength alone, consider shifting weight through the legs and using larger muscle groups. Step to change direction instead of twisting the lower back while supporting a load. Leverage and horizontal movement are principles for understanding how forces work.

kaigo-foundation-07-knowledge-1.heading: Knowing a principle is not permission to perform a task
paragraphs: Knowing body mechanics does not mean it is safe to lift a person on your own. Choose the method and number of helpers according to the person’s abilities and pain, the plan, equipment instructions and staff training. For transfers involving someone who needs full assistance, using lifts and similar equipment and avoiding manual lifting is the basic approach.

Even when moving closer or positioning limbs, explain what you will do and avoid strain on joints or skin. Moving with assistive equipment is different from pulling or dragging a person’s body or skin.

kaigo-foundation-07-knowledge-2.heading: Staff health and disaster preparedness
paragraphs: Maintain appropriate eating, sleep, rest and exercise, and seek support rather than dealing with stress or health problems alone. Staff health is one of the conditions for continuing to provide safe care.

Prepare for disasters by checking evacuation routes, supplies, responsibilities and communication methods, and taking part in training. In a fire or another emergency, follow the facility’s procedure to raise the alarm and seek help without waiting to finish records. Do not independently attempt actions for which you have not been trained.

kaigo-foundation-07-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s practice situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Hasebe has changed the afternoon plan and wants to read independently in the room instead of joining music time. The requests are to find the bookmarked page and report the absence. Do not extend the assistance to reading aloud or insisting on participation.

kaigo-foundation-07-dialogue.heading: Conversation in context
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Hasebe has changed the afternoon plan and wants to read independently in the room instead of joining music time. The requests are to find the bookmarked page and report the absence. Do not extend the assistance to reading aloud or insisting on participation.
Kenichi Hasebe: I’d like to stay here and read today instead of going to the music activity.
Care worker: You’d like to read in your room today, is that right? Is there anything you’d like help with?
Kenichi Hasebe: I can read on my own. Just help me find where I left off yesterday.
Care worker: You’d like help finding the page, then. Is there anything marking it?
Kenichi Hasebe: There’s a blue bookmark. Please tell the activity coordinator I won’t be there.
Care worker: I’ll open the book at the blue bookmark and tell the coordinator only that you won’t be joining today.
Kenichi Hasebe: Yes, please. I’d like some quiet until I finish reading.
Care worker: Of course. Once I’ve opened the page, I’ll leave you to read on your own. Please call me if you need anything else.

kaigo-foundation-07-transfer-legacy.heading: Apply the ideas in another situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] The person wants to do the crossword independently and has asked staff to bring writing materials and report their absence from an activity.
Approach: Confirm which materials are needed and what to say in the message. Let the person solve the crossword.
Example response: I’ll bring your writing materials and let the person in charge know you won’t be joining the activity. You’d like to do the crossword yourself, is that right?
Limits of support: Do not supply answers that were not requested or insist that the person join the activity.

kaigo-foundation-07-reading.heading: Read records and messages
paragraphs: Hasebe will not join today’s music activity and wishes to read in the room. Hasebe will do the reading independently. Staff were asked to find the page with the blue bookmark and tell the activity coordinator about today’s absence.

kaigo-language-transfer-241.heading: What is not being done now and what will be discussed later
paragraphs: [Text created for learning] Person receiving care: “I’d like to rest now, so please discuss airing the room with me this afternoon.” Care worker: “We won’t do it now, then. We’ll discuss it this afternoon.”

kaigo-foundation-01-words.heading: Vocabulary and useful expressions
paragraphs: 介護職員（かいごしょくいん） — Care worker: a staff member who provides necessary help with daily activities and supports the person’s everyday life.
担当（たんとう） — Being responsible for a particular task or for supporting a person receiving care.
看護師（かんごし） — Nurse: a professional who provides nursing care and assists with medical care.
挨拶（あいさつ） — Greeting: expressing goodwill through words or behavior when meeting, parting or on similar occasions.
都合（つごう） — Convenience: how well a time or arrangement fits someone’s schedule and circumstances.
尊厳（そんげん） — Dignity: the worth of being valued as an individual. It does not change with the amount of help a person needs.
自己決定（じこけってい） — Self-determination: choosing and deciding matters concerning one’s own life.
Useful expression: Yes, I’m Tanaka, a care worker. I’m assigned to your room today. It’s nice to meet you.
Useful expression: That’s right, I’m a care worker. If you’d like to speak to a nurse, I can put you in touch with the nurse responsible.

kaigo-foundation-02-words.heading: Vocabulary and useful expressions
paragraphs: 希望（きぼう） — Wishes: what the person would like to do or have happen.
新聞（しんぶん） — Newspaper: a publication containing news and other articles.
眼鏡（めがね） — Glasses: an aid worn on the face to help with vision.

kaigo-depth-01.heading: Protective equipment and separating clean from contaminated items
paragraphs: Choose protective equipment according to what you may touch and what may splash during the task. Consider gloves for contact with blood, body fluids or excreta; an apron or gown for contamination of clothing; and a mask or eye protection for splashes toward the relevant areas. The same complete set, including a cap, is not necessarily needed for every care task. The outside of used protective equipment may be contaminated.

Perform hand hygiene before providing care and check that the necessary protective equipment is fitted properly. When moving from a dirty task to a clean task, or to another person receiving care, remove gloves appropriately and perform hand hygiene. If the next task requires gloves, use a new pair.

When removing gloves, avoid touching the contaminated outside with bare hands. Fold the contaminated surface inward and discard the gloves in the designated place. Handle a mask by its straps or ties without touching the front. Avoid lowering a mask to your chin and then putting it back into use. Follow the sequence for putting on and removing protective equipment that you have been trained to use at your facility.

Touching a clean towel container or nurse call button with gloves that have touched excreta can spread contamination. Keep clean items and waste in separate places, and prepare what you need beforehand. Do not skip hand hygiene after removing gloves.
This section teaches the reasons for these practices and their limits. In actual care, follow the person’s condition, facility procedures, product instructions and your training.

kaigo-depth-02.heading: Handwashing and alcohol-based hand rubbing
paragraphs: Washing with running water and soap removes dirt by rinsing it away. This differs from rubbing the hands with an alcohol-based product. Wash your hands when there is visible dirt; do not assume alcohol alone can deal with all dirt or infection risks. Check the facility’s method for the pathogen and task involved.

For handwashing, wet your hands, use soap and wash the palms, backs of the hands, between the fingers, thumbs, fingertips, around the nails and wrists. Rinse and dry appropriately. For alcohol-based hand rubbing, use the amount specified for the product, distribute it over the necessary areas and rub until dry. Do not wipe it off partway through with paper or another material.

Rings, watches and similar items may interfere with cleaning, so check workplace rules. Palms that look clean do not prove that the thumbs and fingertips have been treated too. Touching a contaminated object after hand hygiene can contaminate the hands again.
This explanation is for learning. Do not independently change product-specific amounts, contact times or infection prevention measures. Follow facility procedures and training in actual work.

kaigo-depth-03.heading: Arrange safe working conditions instead of relying on force
paragraphs: The relationship between the base of support and the center of gravity helps explain postural stability. Relevant principles include positioning the feet appropriately apart, bringing the working position closer to the body and using large muscle groups, including those of the legs and hips. These principles do not mean that good posture enables one worker to lift another person’s entire weight alone.

Before helping someone move, check what they can do, any pain, the equipment, the number of workers needed and the method. Adjust the bed to a height suitable for the task. Reposition your feet to face the direction of movement rather than pulling while twisting your lower back.

Even when applying the principle of moving body parts together, do not force a painful or paralyzed joint to bend. Do not use a weak arm as a handle. Consider fulcrums and the direction of force within a safe plan. Moving someone horizontally with equipment that reduces friction is different from dragging their skin against a sheet.

Do not confuse dragging someone by the armpits or wrists with support using equipment. If the strain is too great, review the method, equipment and staffing. For situations such as transferring someone who needs full assistance, prioritize lifts or other equipment and consider methods that do not rely on manually lifting the person.
The actual method depends on the individual care plan, the person’s condition, equipment instructions and training. Do not attempt an unfamiliar transfer based only on this text.
